title: Complex Images & Data Visualization 📊
description: Make charts, graphs, and infographics accessible through long descriptions, tables, and ARIA.

slides.title: The Challenge of Data Visualizations 📈
slides.content:
Charts and graphs convey data visually. For blind users, this data must be available as **structured text**.

Approaches:

* Provide a **data table** adjacent to the chart – the most universal alternative.
* Use a **long description** (see l1) that summarizes trends and key values.
* For interactive charts (SVG/Canvas), use ARIA to make data points navigable.

The goal: a blind user should be able to extract the same insights as a sighted user.

quizData.question: What is the most robust way to make a bar chart accessible?

options.text: Include a data table with the same information

quizData.explanation: A data table gives precise, navigable data for screen reader users.

slides.title: Accessible Infographics 🗺️
slides.content:
Infographics combine text and visuals to tell a story. Accessibility:

* The `alt` text should summarize the key message (e.g., "5 ways climate change affects oceans").
* A long description or transcript should convey all the information in a linear, logical order.
* Break down complex parts into lists, headings, and paragraphs.
* Consider creating an HTML version of the infographic as the primary content, with the image as decorative.

slides.title: Infographic as HTML
slides.codeSnippet:
5 Ways to Reduce Carbon

  1. Drive less: reduce emissions by 20%
    2. ...

quizData.question: What is the ideal way to present an infographic accessibly?

options.text: An image with detailed alt text
Build the content in semantic HTML and use the image decoratively

quizData.explanation: HTML provides native accessibility; the image can supplement for visual appeal.

slides.title: Canvas & WebGL Accessibility ⚠️
slides.content:
The `<canvas>` element is an accessibility black hole – content drawn on it is invisible to screen readers.

* Provide a **fallback** inside the canvas: `<canvas>Your browser doesn't support canvas</canvas>` (only shown if canvas fails, not useful).
* Use **`aria-label`** on the canvas for a general description.
* For complex canvas apps (games, visualizations), build a parallel **accessibility tree** using off‑screen DOM elements that mirror the canvas state.

This is advanced; libraries like **react‑konva** have accessibility add‑ons.

quizData.question: How can you make a `<canvas>` chart partially accessible?

options.text: Provide a data table next to it and use `aria-label` on the canvas

quizData.explanation: A data table plus `aria-label` gives basic context, but full accessibility requires mirroring in the DOM.

slides.title: Interactive Maps & Geovisualizations 🗺️
slides.content:
Maps are complex. Provide:

* A text list of locations with addresses.
* Keyboard navigable markers (each with `aria-label`).
* The ability to zoom and pan with keyboard (+/- keys, arrow keys).

Leaflet and other mapping libraries have accessibility plugins.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Think in layers
When designing data‑rich visuals, always ask: 'If I couldn't see this, what would I need to know?' Then provide that as text.
